claim: Collagen export from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) requires TANGO1, COPII coats, and retrograde fusion of ERGIC membranes.
source: Collagen export from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) requires TANGO1, COPII coats, and retrograde fusion of ERGIC membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known requirement for collagen export, supported by prior research.

claim: TANGO1 forms a ring that corrals COPII coats.
source: TANGO1 is known to form a ring that corrals COPII coats
evidence: This is stated as known information in the abstract, referencing prior work.

claim: A TANGO1 ring is organized by its radial interaction with COPII, and lateral interactions with cTAGE5, TANGO1-short or itself.
source: Our data reveal that a TANGO1 ring is organized by its radial interaction with COPII, and lateral interactions with cTAGE5, TANGO1-short or itself.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1 recruits ERGIC membranes for collagen export via the NRZ (NBAS/RINT1/ZW10) tether complex.
source: Of particular interest is the finding that TANGO1 recruits ERGIC membranes for collagen export via the NRZ (NBAS/RINT1/ZW10) tether complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1 couples retrograde membrane flow to anterograde cargo transport.
source: Therefore, TANGO1 couples retrograde membrane flow to anterograde cargo transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding about NRZ complex recruitment.

claim: Without the NRZ complex, the TANGO1 ring does not assemble.
source: Without the NRZ complex, the TANGO1 ring does not assemble, suggesting its role in nucleating or stabilising this process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing disrupted ring formation upon NRZ depletion.

claim: The NRZ complex plays a role in nucleating or stabilising TANGO1 ring assembly.
source: Without the NRZ complex, the TANGO1 ring does not assemble, suggesting its role in nucleating or stabilising this process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: Coordinated capture of COPII coats, cTAGE5, TANGO1-short, and tethers by TANGO1 assembles a collagen export machine at the ER.
source: Thus, coordinated capture of COPII coats, cTAGE5, TANGO1-short, and tethers by TANGO1 assembles a collagen export machine at the ER.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Collagens represent nearly 25% of the dry weight of the mammalian body.
source: Collagens, the most abundant secretory cargo in mammals - representing nearly 25% of the dry weight of the mammalian body, are some of the most challenging of all secretory cargoes (Kadler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Kadler et al., 2007.

claim: Collagens in the ER fold and trimerise into rigid, rod-like elements of up to 400 nm in length.
source: First, in a complex multi-step process, collagens in the ER fold and trimerise into rigid, rod-like elements (Ishikawa et al., 2015; Kadler, 2017) of up to 400 nm in length (Burgeson et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple sources.

claim: Assembled collagens are too large to fit into generic COPII-coated vesicles that are usually less than 90 nm in diameter.
source: Second, assembled collagens are too large to fit into generic COPII-coated vesicles that are usually less than 90 nm in diameter (Malhotra and Erlmann, 2015; Miller and Schekman, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TANGO1 is an ER exit site (ERES)-localized, transmembrane protein required for export of collagen.
source: TANGO1 is an ER exit site (ERES)-localized, transmembrane protein required for export of collagen and other bulky protein components of the extracellular matrix such as Dumpy (Saito et al., 2009; Ríos-Barrera et al., 2017; Maiers et al., 2017; Tomoishi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: TANGO1 is required for export of bulky protein components of the extracellular matrix such as Dumpy.
source: TANGO1 is an ER exit site (ERES)-localized, transmembrane protein required for export of collagen and other bulky protein components of the extracellular matrix such as Dumpy (Saito et al., 2009; Ríos-Barrera et al., 2017; Maiers et al., 2017; Tomoishi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TANGO1 is a type one single-pass transmembrane protein of 1907 amino acids.
source: TANGO1 is a type one single-pass transmembrane protein of 1907 amino acids, localised to ER exit sites.
evidence: This is a description of TANGO1 structure stated in the figure legend.

claim: TANGO1 has an N-terminal lumenal SH3-like domain that interacts with collagen via the chaperone, HSP47.
source: TANGO1 has an N-terminal lumenal SH3-like domain that interacts with collagen (Saito et al., 2009) via the chaperone, HSP47 (Ishikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TANGO1 CC1 is used by TANGO1 to recruit ERGIC membranes for producing a collagen carrier.
source: CC1 is used by TANGO1 to recruit ERGIC membranes for producing a collagen carrier (Santos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: TANGO1 CC2 binds to a similar coiled-coil domain in cTAGE5.
source: CC2 binds to a similar coiled-coil domain in cTAGE5 (18).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The TANGO1 proline-rich domain (PRD) binds ER exit site machinery Sec23 and Sec16.
source: The proline-rich domain (PRD) binds ER exit site machinery Sec23 (Saito et al., 2009; Ma and Goldberg, 2016) and Sec16 (Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Alternative splicing of TANGO1 results in a short isoform, TANGO1-short, lacking the lumenal domain.
source: Alternative splicing of TANGO1 results in a short isoform, TANGO1-short (Wilson et al., 2011), lacking the lumenal domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: cTAGE5 CC1 recruits Sec12.
source: Via its CC1 it recruits Sec12 (Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: cTAGE5 and TANGO1/TANGO1-short interact through their respective CC2 domains.
source: cTAGE5 and TANGO1/TANGO1-short interact through their respective CC2 domains.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the figure legend.

claim: The cTAGE5 CC2 interacts with the retrograde v-SNARE Sec22.
source: In addition, the cTAGE5 CC2 also interacts with the retrograde v-SNARE Sec22 (Fan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The cTAGE5 PRD interacts with Sec23.
source: Like the TANGO1/TANGO1-short PRDs, the cTAGE5 PRD also interacts with Sec23 (Ma and Goldberg, 2016; Saito et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Full length TANGO1 forms distinct rings of somewhat uniform shape and size.
source: Full length TANGO1 formed distinct rings of somewhat uniform shape and size (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: TANGO1ΔPRD assembles into rings that are smaller than full-length TANGO1 rings.
source: Surprisingly, TANGO1ΔPRD also assembled into rings, but with two clear differences. First, rings were smaller (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data and quantification presented in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1ΔPRD rings appear fused with each other to form either a planar tessellation or long linear assemblies.
source: and second, some rings appeared fused with each other to form either a planar tessellation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) or long linear assemblies (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data presented in the figures.

claim: Rings formed by TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔPRD have a similar shape as measured by aspect ratio.
source: By this measure, rings formed by TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔPRD had a similar shape (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of microscopy data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Depletion of Sec23A reduces collagen export from the ER.
source: As expected, collagen export from the ER was reduced in Sec23A-depleted cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Depletion of Sec23A causes TANGO1 to form multiple seemingly fused rings assembled in planar arrays.
source: While TANGO1 in control cells was often visualised in rings (Figure 2G), depletion of Sec23A appeared to phenocopy our results with TANGO1ΔPRD, showing multiple seemingly fused rings of TANGO1 assembled in planar arrays (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), quantified in Figure 2I.
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy comparing control and Sec23A-depleted cells.

claim: cTAGE5 localises along the rings delineated by TANGO1.
source: We visualised TANGO1 and cTAGE5 in RDEB/FB/C7 cells by STED microscopy. Due to the low quality of commercially available anti-cTAGE5 antibodies for immunofluorescence, we were unable to visualise the localisation of cTAGE5 as clearly as TANGO1, nonetheless cTAGE5 clearly localised along the rings delineated by TANGO1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: TANGO1ΔCC2 assembles into misshapen structures.
source: STED microscopy revealed that, in contrast to full length TANGO1 (Figure 3C), TANGO1ΔCC2 assembled into misshapen structures (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data.

claim: Rings formed by TANGO1ΔCC2 are more variable in size than those formed by full length TANGO1.
source: Rings formed by TANGO1ΔCC2 were more variable in size (Figure 3E, Table 1) and shape (Figure 3F) than those formed by full length TANGO1.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of microscopy data presented in the figure and table.

claim: Depletion of cTAGE5 blocks collagen secretion.
source: As expected, in RDEB/FB/C7 fibroblasts depleted of cTAGE5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), collagen secretion was blocked (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from collagen secretion assays.

claim: In cells depleted of cTAGE5, TANGO1 rings are misassembled and form unusual shapes.
source: TANGO1 structures phenocopied TANGO1ΔCC2 structures in 2H5 cells: rings of TANGO1 were misassembled (Figure 3G) and formed unusual shapes, without considerably altering the number of rings observed (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy of cTAGE5-depleted cells.

claim: TANGO1-FLAG co-immunoprecipitates with TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔPRD, but not with TANGO1ΔCC2 or TANGO1ΔCC1.
source: We observed (Figure 4A) that TANGO1-FLAG was immunoprecipitated by TANGO1 and TANGO1ΔPRD, but not by TANGO1ΔCC2 (Figure 4A) or TANGO1ΔCC1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental result from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: TANGO1Δ1255–1295 does not immunoprecipitate TANGO1-FLAG.
source: Only TANGO1Δ1255–1295 did not immunoprecipitate TANGO1-FLAG (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental result from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: TANGO1ΔCC1 and TANGO1Δ1255–1295 cannot form rings.
source: In line with our predictions, TANGO1ΔCC1 or TANGO1Δ1255–1295 could not form rings; of the 16 and 15 cells examined respectively, there were few discernible polymeric assemblies of TANGO1 (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy experiments.

claim: TANGO1Δ1296–1336 forms distinct, readily detectable, independent rings similar to full length TANGO1.
source: while TANGO1Δ1296–1336 behaved as full length TANGO1, forming distinct, readily detectable, independent rings (Figure 4E) of similar size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and shape (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) as TANGO1.
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy and quantitative analysis.

claim: TANGO1-TANGO1 interactions mediated by amino acids 1255–1295 are required to maintain ring integrity.
source: These data indicate that TANGO1-TANGO1 interactions (Figure 4F), mediated by amino acids 1255–1295, are required to maintain ring integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on TANGO1 self-association and ring formation.

claim: Mitochondria expressing mit-Δ1255–1295 show no recruitment of ERGIC-53-containing membranes.
source: To our surprise, mitochondria expressing mit-Δ1255–1295 showed no recruitment of ERGIC-53-containing membranes (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the mitochondrial targeting assay.

claim: mit-Δ1296–1336 functions as the TEER domain and recruits ERGIC membranes.
source: In contrast, mit-Δ1296–1336 still functioned as the TEER domain and recruited ERGIC membranes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the mitochondrial targeting assay.

claim: The minimal TEER is the same forty amino acids required for the self-association of TANGO1.
source: This tells us that the minimal TEER is exactly the same forty amino acids we identified in the previous section, as those required for the self-association of TANGO1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the TEER domain mapping with the self-association domain mapping.

claim: The tether protein RINT1 localises to one or two puncta at rings of TANGO1, occasionally adjacent to ERGIC-53-containing membranes.
source: As in previous sections, we imaged TANGO1 in RDEB/FB/C7 cells, with Sec31 and RINT1 by confocal microscopy (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and, by STED microscopy observed the tether protein RINT1 localised to one or two puncta at rings of TANGO1, occasionally adjacent to ERGIC-53-containing membranes (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy data.

claim: Full length TANGO1 and TANGO1Δ1296–1336 immunoprecipitate all three proteins that form the NRZ tether (NBAS, RINT1, ZW10).
source: We saw that full length TANGO1 and TANGO1Δ1296–1336 immunoprecipitated all three of the proteins that form the tether (NBAS, RINT1, ZW10) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an experimental result from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: The interaction between TANGO1 and NRZ tether proteins is completely abrogated when using TANGO1Δ1255–1295.
source: This interaction was completely abrogated when we used TANGO1Δ1255–1295 (lacking the minimal TEER domain).
evidence: This is an experimental result from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: Depleting TANGO1, NBAS or RINT1 from RDEB/FB/C7 fibroblasts inhibits collagen VII secretion.
source: Depleting TANGO1, NBAS or RINT1 from RDEB/FB/C7 fibroblasts inhibited collagen VII secretion (Figure 6C–E) and arrested collagen in the ER (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from collagen secretion assays.

claim: In cells depleted of RINT1, NBAS or TANGO1, ERGIC membrane recruitment to collagen accumulations is significantly reduced.
source: In cells depleted of RINT1, NBAS or TANGO1 (Figure 6F,H), we quantified ERGIC recruitment to accumulations of collagen in the ER. In all cases, ERGIC membrane recruitment was significantly reduced (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an experimental result from quantitative microscopy analysis.

claim: TANGO1 recruits ERGIC membranes via the retrograde NRZ MTC to the ERES for collagen export.
source: These data showed a novel function of TANGO1, to recruit ERGIC membranes via the retrograde NRZ MTC to the ERES for collagen export.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on NRZ tether interaction and ERGIC recruitment.

claim: In RDEB/FB/C7 depleted of RINT1, TANGO1 rings are completely disrupted.
source: In RDEB/FB/C7 depleted of RINT1, TANGO1 rings were completely disrupted (siCTRL vs. siRINT1 Figure 7A vs. B).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy of RINT1-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of NBAS or ZW10 results in TANGO1 rings being observed far less frequently.
source: We individually depleted each of the other two proteins in the MTC (NBAS or ZW10) and checked for the ability of TANGO1 to assemble into rings in RDEB/FB/C7 fibroblasts. As seen after depleting cells of RINT1, rings were observed far less frequently (quantified in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an observation from STED microscopy and quantification.

claim: The NRZ tether has no effect on the association of TANGO1 and TANGO1-short in a stable complex.
source: We observed that the NRZ tether had no effect on the association of TANGO1 and TANGO1-short in a stable complex (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is an experimental result from sequential co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: The NRZ tether is required for TANGO1 to assemble into a ring.
source: These data showed that the NRZ tether is required for TANGO1 to assemble into a ring
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing disrupted ring formation upon NRZ depletion.

claim: Stable complexes of TANGO1, cTAGE5 and TANGO1-short recruit the NRZ tether.
source: and indicated that stable complexes of TANGO1, cTAGE5 and TANGO1-short, recruit the tether.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequential co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: TANGO1 functionally and physically couples anterograde to retrograde traffic at an ERES.
source: A critical aspect of TANGO1 biology is that it functionally and physically couples anterograde to retrograde traffic at an ERES, coupling two successive compartments in the secretory pathway, allowing for more rapid and efficient cargo transport between the compartments (Nogueira et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established aspect of TANGO1 biology with citations.

claim: HSP47 selectively recognises triple helical (export-competent) collagen.
source: TANGO1 recruits collagen via HSP47 – a chaperone that selectively recognises triple helical (export-competent) collagen (Koide et al., 2000; Tasab et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TANGO1 contains a full transmembrane domain and a second membrane-inserted loop.
source: TANGO1 contains a full transmembrane domain and a second membrane-inserted loop, which partially inserts into the inner leaflet of the ER membrane.
evidence: This is a structural description of TANGO1 stated in the manuscript.

claim: The lumenal part of TANGO1 contains a coiled-coil domain and an SH3-like domain at the N terminus.
source: The lumenal part contains a coiled-coil domain and, at the N terminus, an SH3-like domain.
evidence: This is a structural description of TANGO1 stated in the manuscript.

claim: The cytoplasmic part of TANGO1 is composed of two coiled-coil domains (CC1 and CC2) followed by a C-terminal proline-rich domain (PRD).
source: The cytoplasmic part of TANGO1 is composed of two coiled-coil domains (CC1 and CC2) followed by a C-terminal proline-rich domain (PRD).
evidence: This is a structural description of TANGO1 stated in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1-short is composed of 785 amino acids that arise from the same exons that encode the cytoplasmic domains of TANGO1.
source: TANGO1-short is a spliced isoform of TANGO1. It is composed of 785 amino acids that arise from the same exons that encode the cytoplasmic domains of TANGO1.
evidence: This is a description of TANGO1-short structure stated in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1-short contains only 15 amino acids at the N terminus, within the ER lumen.
source: The sequence of TANGO1-short differs in the membrane-inserted helix, and it contains only 15 amino acids at the N terminus, within the ER lumen.
evidence: This is a structural description of TANGO1-short stated in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1-short lacks any capacity to interact directly with cargoes.
source: It therefore lacks any capacity to interact directly with cargoes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural description of TANGO1-short lacking the lumenal domain.

claim: cTAGE5 is composed of 804 amino acids, with a short lumenal stretch of 38 amino acids, followed by a single transmembrane domain.
source: cTAGE5 is composed of 804 amino acids, with a short lumenal stretch of 38 amino acids, followed by a single transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is a structural description of cTAGE5 stated in the manuscript.

claim: The organisation of cytoplasmic domains in cTAGE5 is the same as TANGO1, with two coiled-coil domains and a PRD.
source: The organisation of cytoplasmic domains is the same as TANGO1, with two coiled-coil domains and a PRD.
evidence: This is a structural description of cTAGE5 stated in the manuscript.

claim: All three TANGO1 family members bind each other and Sec23.
source: From the published data on these proteins, we can conclude that all three family members bind each other and Sec23.
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge from published data.

claim: cTAGE5 binds Sec12 and Sec22.
source: cTAGE5 binds Sec12 and Sec22.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from published data.

claim: TANGO1 does not bind Sec12.
source: TANGO1 (and therefore TANGO1-short) does not bind Sec12.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from published data.

claim: Only TANGO1 can bind cargo in the lumen.
source: Of these proteins, only TANGO1 can bind cargo in the lumen.
evidence: This is stated based on the structural features of the TANGO1 family proteins.

claim: TANGO1 organises into rings of up to 300 nm diameter, which corral COPII coats at the ERES.
source: A newly discovered feature of TANGO1 is its lateral organisation into rings of up to 300 nm diameter, which corral COPII coats at the ERES (Raote et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a recently discovered feature with a citation.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of the TANGO1-family of proteins act as a single unit and any one can assemble into a ring.
source: These data suggest that the cytoplasmic domains of the TANGO1-family of proteins act as a single unit and any one can assemble into a ring, however TANGO1 brings cargo to the exit site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on TANGO1ΔPRD ring formation.

claim: Overexpressing cytoplasmic isoforms (either TANGO1-short or cTAGE5) would increase the capacity of an ERES to export cargo.
source: This suggests that overexpressing cytoplasmic isoforms (either TANGO1-short or cTAGE5) would increase the capacity of an ERES to export cargo, however TANGO1 is the only protein with the capacity to bring cargo to ERES.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Collagen secreted in the absence of TANGO1 might be in an unfolded or unassembled form.
source: Collagen secreted in the absence of TANGO1 might thus be in an unfolded or unassembled form.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on TANGO1's role in cargo selection.

claim: TANGO1 rings could be represented as a multimeric assembly of units of TANGO1 family proteins that assemble into a fence.
source: Based on our super-resolution microscopy images, we hypothesise that TANGO1 rings could be represented as a multimeric assembly of units of TANGO1 family proteins (TANGO1, TANGO1-short and cTAGE5) that assemble into a fence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the super-resolution microscopy observations.

claim: The NRZ tether is a multi-subunit tether complex (MTC) that assembles at the surface of the ER.
source: NRZ tether is a multi-subunit tether complex (MTC) that assembles at the surface of the ER (Ren et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The NRZ tether is required for retrograde capture of membranes.
source: is required for retrograde capture of membranes (Aoki et al., 2009; Arasaki et al., 2006; Hirose et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The NRZ tether partially localises to ER exit sites.
source: partially localises to ER exit sites (Schröter et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Mutations in NBAS are linked to dysregulated collagen secretion in atypical osteogenesis imperfecta.
source: Mutations in another component NBAS, are linked to dysregulated collagen secretion in atypical osteogenesis imperfecta (DDD Study et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: A fence of TANGO1 can be described as a filament held together by lateral protein–protein interactions.
source: First, based on our observations of TANGO1 rings by STED microscopy (Raote et al., 2017), (Figure 2), and our data indicating the different protein–protein interactions between the members of the TANGO1 family, we propose that a fence of TANGO1 can be described as a filament, held together by these lateral protein–protein interactions, which normally surrounds COPII patches at the ERES (Maeda et al., 2017; Saito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: TANGO1 rings could serve as a mould to impose a cylindrical curvature at the base of a growing carrier by coupling to the first layer of the COPII coat.
source: Furthermore, TANGO1 rings could serve as a mould to impose a cylindrical curvature at the base of a growing carrier by coupling to the first layer of the COPII coat (Figure 8A,B), as proposed by Ma and Goldberg (Ma and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and prior work.
